extracted.intended_audience: USPTO rulemakers, patent practitioners, and policymakers (patent bar and stakeholders)
extracted.subtask_description: A professional organization's detailed public comments on the USPTO Notices of Proposed Rulemaking implementing AIA post-grant proceedings (inter partes review, post-grant review, covered business-method review, and derivation). Recommends procedural, evidentiary, and rulemaking standards the Office should adopt or revise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry forward interference evidentiary rules for new AIA proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board should not discard its long-standing rules and practices used to decide interferences; many existing interference rules will be required for derivation proceedings and the new trial-type proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New AIA proceedings will involve qualitatively different evidence (e.g., public use, on sale, foreign evidence) and will often turn on no-document evidence and expert inferences. The Board should carry forward interference regulations to provide default procedures (live testimony, cross-examination, credibility assessment) and to ensure the Office can fairly develop and adjudicate complex factual disputes rather than treating these as examiner-style reexaminations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of persuasion on petitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules for initiating an inter partes review, post-grant review, or transitional covered business methods patent review are silent as to allocation of burden of persuasion; IEEE-USA requests that implementing regulations clarify that the petitioner must bear the burden of persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although proposed §§ 42.104, 42.204 and 42.304 allocate the burden of going forward to the petitioner, USPTO should explicitly state that the petitioner also bears the burden of persuasion consistent with 35 U.S.C. §§ 316(e) and 326(e), and that the burden does not shift to the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require proof and corroboration in opening petitions for 'on sale' and 'public use' evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions invoking 'on sale' and 'public use' prior art should require proof in the opening Petition, including evidence of corroboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral testimony or affidavits regarding public use or on-sale evidence must be corroborated; the petition must specify where each element of the construed claim is found in the prior art. Documents used to corroborate testimony must be sufficiently complete, clear, and detailed to show that each and every element of a claim is present. Proposed amendment to § 42.204(b)(4)-(5): (4) specify how the construed claim is unpatentable and require corroboration for no-document evidence; (5) provide the exhibit number of supporting/corroborating evidence and state relevance and specific portions relied upon. The Board may exclude or give no weight to evidence where relevance or supporting portions are not identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard should reflect adjudicative nature (use Phillips/Markman)
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR and PGR trials are not examinations, and the claim construction rules should reflect that—they should use claim construction 'in light of the specification and prosecution history' (district court standard), not the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) used for examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI is an examination tool appropriate where iterative amendment is available; IPR/PGR provide only limited amendment opportunities and are adjudicative in nature. Applying BRI would unfairly broaden claim scope for validity determinations and create conflicts with concurrent district court infringement proceedings. Amend proposed §§ 42.100(b) and 42.200(b) to adopt the federal district court (Phillips/Markman) standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish an ascertainable standard for 'charged with infringement' in transitional CBM jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO should publish some 'ascertainable standard' to interpret the phrase 'charged with infringement' in proposed § 42.302(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two possible standards exist (the pre-MedImmune narrower standard and the post-MedImmune broader standard for declaratory judgment jurisdiction). The USPTO should pick a standard and state it in the regulation so parties have clear, ascertainable rules for CBM petition eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify procedures and safeguards for expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRMs are silent on many issues concerning expert testimony; the rules should address voir dire, Daubert-type challenges, live testimony, disclosure of expert evidence, and potential appointment of neutral experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current § 42.65 (Expert testimony; tests and data) is inadequate for the expanded use of experts in IPR/PGR/CBM. IEEE-USA raises questions: Will experts be subject to voir dire and Daubert challenges? Will live testimony be required to assess demeanor/credibility? What disclosure format will be used (expert reports analogous to Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2))? If petition relies on expert testimony at petition stage, how may the patent owner challenge it? Should the Board appoint neutral experts under a Fed. R. Ev. 706 analog? The rules should provide clear procedures to ensure integrity and fairness of expert evidence and to survive judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide fair timing and extension mechanisms for patent owner replies
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO should recognize inherent unfairness where challengers have ample time to prepare petitions but patent owners face constrained schedules; the rules should allow reasonable time or extensions to reply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding appropriate technical experts and investigating contested foreign 'on sale' or 'public use' evidence can take months; patent owners should be permitted extensions for good cause or in the interest of justice. The USPTO may also promulgate rules to deny or strictly scrutinize petitions relying solely on contested foreign on-sale/public-use evidence where timely development of rebuttal evidence is impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery procedures must match trial-type nature of proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the new proceedings are trial-type and involve evidence unlike past reexaminations, discovery rules must allow development of evidentiary records analogous to litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board should not underestimate the work required to develop a case (gathering evidence, depositions, expert development). Proposed discovery rules (e.g., § 42.51 referenced) should be robust enough to allow parties to vet no-document evidence, adduce and challenge expert testimony, and develop facts that would otherwise require foreign legal processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing estoppel beyond statutory authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: The Umbrella Rule proposes estoppel provisions that may exceed statutory limits; the PTO should not impose estoppel beyond what Congress authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed regulations should be revised to align estoppel narrowly with statutory language and intent, avoiding broader de facto estoppel that would unfairly limit parties' future rights beyond AIA provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation rules must reflect full elements of derivation law
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed derivation rules ignore critical elements in the law of derivation and are therefore incomplete; they should be revised to include these elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific recommendations (section II.A-II.E) include clarifying that the Board would normally not defer action on derivation petitions, clarifying the process for determining the scope of derived subject matter, implementing procedures for correcting the name of the inventor in derivation proceedings, and adding implementing regulations for showing derivation over non-patent disclosures that appear to be prior art but are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require claim construction submissions in derivation petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rules to require submission of claim construction in derivation proceedings are unnecessary and inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission of claim construction by one party often invites burdensome rebuttals; the identity of language of a count (in derivation contexts) typically provides sufficient basis for a derivation petition without requiring formal claim construction submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comply with Administrative Procedure Act in characterization of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost all provisions of these regulations are 'legislative' rather than 'interpretative' and 'procedural' rather than 'substantive'; the USPTO must correctly characterize and follow APA obligations for rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office should acknowledge the nature of the rules, provide reasoned explanations, and follow APA notice-and-comment and procedural requirements when promulgating legislative/procedural rules rather than treating them as interpretative guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fulfill disclosure obligations under IQA, PRA, e-Government Act, and EO 12,866
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRMs neglect to disclose significant material information required by the Information Quality Act, Paperwork Reduction Act, e-Government Act, and Executive Order 12,866; USPTO must correct these omissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must provide data, analyses, and objective support for claims in the NPRM; for example, failure to disclose assumptions and analyses underlying burden estimates and economic effects must be remedied and made available for public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform a Regulatory Impact Analysis for economically significant rules
rubrics_metrics.description: These regulations are economically significant under Executive Order 12,866 and require a Regulatory Impact Analysis; the USPTO should provide careful analysis and not avoid obligations via exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO must analyze costs and benefits pursuant to OMB Circular A-4, use objective methods (disclose numerical assumptions), consider growth in filings, consider economic effects on small entities, and avoid manipulating thresholds to evade analysis. An accurate RIA is essential for planning, staffing, and public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide objectively supported Paperwork Reduction Act burden estimates and minimize burden
rubrics_metrics.description: PRA requires specific, objectively supported estimates of paperwork burden; the NPRMs' estimates are unsupported and biased too low and must be corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proper statistical measures (mean, not median) for attorney hourly rates; include all relevant costs (in-house client costs, document production infrastructure, litigation-related changes to prosecution practice); account for year-on-year growth; rely on reproducible, transparent data sources rather than unreliable surveys; tailor regulations to minimize respondent burden and only require information with 'practical utility.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate attorney billing rate assumptions (mean, senior rates) in cost estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO's use of the median attorney rate ($340) is analytically wrong and too low for the proceedings; mean and senior practitioner rates should be used instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceedings will be handled by more-senior attorneys with higher billing rates; using medians underestimates total burden. PRA and EO analyses must use the mean cost to estimate total annual reporting and recordkeeping burden as required by regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider collateral economic impacts and effects on small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO estimates ignore many economic impacts (e.g., costs inside client companies, effects on licensees and small entities) and thus understate regulatory effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses must include non-attorney costs (document production, business impacts), consider entities on both sides of proceedings (small patentees and small challengers), and include effects on prosecution behavior induced by the new rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure accurate characterization of public comments and provide reasoned responses
rubrics_metrics.description: IEEE-USA requests that the USPTO take care to characterize all comments accurately and answer them fairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mischaracterizing comments and responding only to mischaracterizations is self-defeating and may render resultant regulations unenforceable; the Office should provide thoughtful, reasoned responses to actual public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Information Quality correction requests as comments and address them in the final rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Under USPTO Information Quality Guidelines, a proper request concerning information disseminated during the comment period will be treated as a comment filed on that proposed rulemaking and be addressed in the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IEEE-USA requests correction in USPTO submissions to OMB under the PRA and in the final rule publication when Information Quality issues are identified, and requests the Office provide an information-quality ticket number in reply.
